title: Pathophysiology
summary: Why disease does what it does, from a single injured cell to shock, sepsis, heart attack, and organ failure — every mechanism traced to what you will actually see in an emergency department.

lessons.title: Where disease starts: the injured cell
lessons.body:
## Every disease is a cell problem first

A cell under stress does one of three things. It adapts, it gets injured and recovers, or it dies. Everything you will see in an emergency department is one of those three happening in enough cells at once to change how a person looks.

## The five adaptations

- **Hypertrophy**: existing cells get bigger. The left ventricle thickens against years of high blood pressure.
- **Hyperplasia**: more cells are made. The prostate enlarges; the endometrium thickens.
- **Atrophy**: cells shrink from disuse or lost blood supply. A limb in a cast for six weeks.
- **Metaplasia**: one mature cell type is swapped for another that tolerates the stress better. Acid reflux turns esophageal squamous cells into columnar cells (Barrett esophagus); smoke turns ciliated airway cells into squamous cells that cannot sweep mucus.
- **Dysplasia**: cells become disordered and abnormal in size and shape. This is no longer normal tissue and it is the last stop that can still reverse if the stress stops. Push further and dysplasia becomes cancer in place, then invasive cancer.

## Reversible versus irreversible injury

Injury starts when ATP production fails. The sodium-potassium pump stops, so sodium and water flood in and the cell swells. The cell switches to anaerobic glycolysis, which makes lactate and drops the pH. Ribosomes fall off and protein synthesis halts. All of this reverses if blood flow returns.

The line is crossed when membranes rupture. Calcium pours into the cytoplasm, lysosomes spill digestive enzymes, and mitochondria are destroyed. Now the cell dies, and its contents leak into the blood. That leak is how the injury is measured: troponin from heart muscle, creatine kinase from skeletal muscle, ALT and AST from liver, lipase from pancreas.

> **Key:** A lab value that measures organ damage is almost always a protein that belongs inside a cell and got out.

## Hypoxia, ischemia, infarction

**Hypoxia** is not enough oxygen in blood that is still flowing, from anemia, lung disease, or carbon monoxide. Glucose still arrives and waste still leaves.

**Ischemia** is not enough blood flow at all. Oxygen and glucose both stop and acid waste piles up, so ischemia kills faster than hypoxia.

**Infarction** is the tissue death that results. The clock runs differently by tissue: brain neurons die in `4-6` minutes, heart muscle becomes irreversibly injured over `20-30` minutes and is largely dead by `6` hours, kidney tubules within about `30` minutes, and skeletal muscle can survive `4-6` hours. That is why a cold pulseless leg has hours and a stroke has minutes.

## Necrosis versus apoptosis

**Necrosis** is uncontrolled death. The cell swells and bursts, contents spill, and inflammation follows. Coagulative necrosis is the pattern in heart and kidney infarcts; liquefactive necrosis is what happens in the brain and in abscesses; caseous necrosis is tuberculosis; fat necrosis is pancreatitis.

**Apoptosis** is programmed, tidy, and energy-requiring. The cell shrinks and is packaged into fragments that neighbors eat, with no inflammation at all. It is how the body removes cells it no longer needs.

Free radicals connect the two. Reactive oxygen molecules are produced during ischemia and in a burst when blood flow returns, which is why reperfusion itself causes a wave of damage.

## Inflammation

Acute inflammation arrives in minutes. Vessels dilate (redness and warmth), become leaky (swelling), and neutrophils crawl out into the tissue. Histamine, bradykinin, prostaglandins, and cytokines such as TNF-alpha and interleukin-1 drive it. The five cardinal signs are redness, heat, swelling, pain, and loss of function.

Chronic inflammation runs for weeks to years with macrophages and lymphocytes, destroying and rebuilding tissue at the same time, and walls off what it cannot kill in a granuloma.

When those same cytokines spill into the bloodstream, the response goes systemic: fever as interleukin-1 and interleukin-6 reset the hypothalamic thermostat through prostaglandin E2, a rising white count, and acute phase proteins such as C-reactive protein. Take that systemic response far enough and it becomes sepsis.

## Healing

Some tissue regenerates (skin, liver, gut lining). Some can only scar (heart, brain), and scar does not contract or think. Healing fails when perfusion is poor, glucose is high, steroids are on board, infection persists, or protein and vitamin C are missing.
keyPoints: Cells adapt (hypertrophy, hyperplasia, atrophy, metaplasia), then become dysplastic, then cancerous.
Injury is reversible until membranes rupture; leaked intracellular proteins like troponin are how we measure the damage.
Ischemia kills faster than hypoxia because glucose delivery and waste removal stop too.
Brain dies in 4-6 minutes, heart over 20-30 minutes, skeletal muscle in 4-6 hours.
Necrosis spills contents and causes inflammation; apoptosis is tidy, programmed, and silent.

checks.q: A patient's troponin rises after a heart attack. What does an elevated troponin physically represent?
choices: A hormone released by the heart in response to stretch
A protein produced by the liver during inflammation
An intracellular contractile protein that leaked out because myocyte membranes ruptured
An antibody the body makes against damaged heart tissue
checks.why: Troponin lives inside the cardiac myocyte as part of the contractile apparatus and can only reach the blood if the cell membrane fails, meaning irreversible injury. BNP is the stretch hormone, CRP is the liver-produced inflammatory protein, and no antibody is involved.

checks.q: Why does ischemia cause cell death faster than hypoxia alone?
choices: Ischemia stops glucose delivery and waste removal as well as oxygen, so acid accumulates
Hypoxia does not affect ATP production
Ischemia directly destroys cell membranes without affecting ATP
Hypoxia only affects the lungs
checks.why: In hypoxia blood still flows, delivering glucose for anaerobic metabolism and carrying lactate away. In ischemia flow has stopped, so substrate is gone and acid builds locally, accelerating injury. Both reduce ATP, and hypoxia affects every tissue, not just lung.

checks.q: A smoker's airway shows ciliated columnar cells replaced by squamous cells. This change is called:
choices: Hyperplasia
Metaplasia
Dysplasia
Apoptosis
checks.why: Metaplasia is the replacement of one mature cell type by another better suited to the stress, and it costs function since squamous cells cannot clear mucus. Hyperplasia is more cells of the same type, dysplasia is disordered abnormal cells, and apoptosis is programmed cell death.

lessons.title: Shock: three stages and four families
lessons.body:
## Shock is a delivery failure, not a blood pressure number

Shock is inadequate delivery of oxygen to tissue for its needs. Blood pressure is a late and unreliable clue, because a young patient can hold a normal pressure while already in serious trouble. Tissue tells the truth first.

Delivery depends on three things: enough blood volume, a pump that works, and vessels that hold tone. Break any one and you get shock.

## The three stages

**Compensated.** Baroreceptors sense falling pressure and fire the sympathetic system. Heart rate rises, vessels constrict, and blood is shunted from skin, gut, and kidney to brain and heart. The kidney releases renin, the body holds salt and water, and the patient looks anxious, pale, cool, and tachycardic with an almost normal blood pressure and a narrowing pulse pressure. This is the stage where treatment works best and where the diagnosis is most often missed.

**Progressive.** Compensation fails. Cells run anaerobically, lactate climbs, and acidosis makes vessels stop responding to catecholamines. Capillaries leak, pressure falls, urine output drops, and the patient becomes confused. Pressors start working less well.

**Irreversible.** Cell membranes fail across multiple organs. Even if blood pressure is restored, the patient dies of multiple organ dysfunction syndrome, which typically starts in the kidneys and the gut because those beds were sacrificed first.

> **Key:** Lactate is the shock marker because it is the byproduct of cells burning fuel without oxygen. Over `2 mmol/L` is abnormal, over `4 mmol/L` is severe, and a lactate that does not fall with treatment predicts death better than any single vital sign.

## The four families

| Type | Mechanism | Skin | Preload | Cardiac output | Resistance |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Hypovolemic | not enough volume | cold, pale | low | low | high |
| Cardiogenic | pump failure | cold, mottled | high | low | high |
| Obstructive | blocked flow | cold | varies | low | high |
| Distributive | vessels dilated | warm early | low | high early | low |

**Hypovolemic** shock is lost volume, either hemorrhagic (trauma, GI bleeding, ruptured ectopic pregnancy, aortic aneurysm) or non-hemorrhagic (vomiting, diarrhea, burns, diabetic ketoacidosis). The fix is replacing what was lost: blood for bleeding, crystalloid for the rest, and stopping the source.

**Cardiogenic** shock is a pump that cannot eject, usually from a large heart attack, and less often from arrhythmia, valve rupture, or myocarditis. The tank is full and backing up into the lungs, so more fluid drowns the patient. The answer is inotropic support and fixing the cause.

**Obstructive** shock is a mechanical block. Cardiac tamponade squeezes the heart from outside so it cannot fill. Tension pneumothorax pushes the mediastinum and kinks the vena cava. Massive pulmonary embolism blocks the outflow of the right ventricle. Fluids and pressors buy minutes; only removing the obstruction works: pericardiocentesis, needle decompression, thrombolysis.

**Distributive** shock is normal volume in a container that suddenly got too big. Septic shock from cytokine-driven vasodilation and capillary leak. Anaphylactic shock from mass histamine release. Neurogenic shock from spinal cord injury above roughly T6, which cuts sympathetic outflow and leaves a patient hypotensive with a **slow** heart rate and warm dry skin, the one shock that does not produce tachycardia. Treatment restores tone: norepinephrine for sepsis, epinephrine for anaphylaxis, vasopressors plus atropine for neurogenic.

> **Trap:** A patient can be in two kinds of shock at once. Trauma plus a spinal injury, or sepsis plus a heart attack. Hypotension that does not respond the way you predicted usually means a second mechanism.

## Why the kidneys and gut fail first

Compensation deliberately sacrifices the kidney and the splanchnic circulation to protect brain and heart. So the earliest measurable organ injury is a falling urine output and a rising creatinine, and the gut lining breaks down and leaks bacteria, which feeds the inflammatory fire and accelerates multiple organ dysfunction.
keyPoints: Shock is inadequate oxygen delivery to tissue; blood pressure falls late, especially in the young.
Compensated shock shows tachycardia, cool pale skin, anxiety, and a narrowing pulse pressure with near-normal pressure.
Lactate over 2 mmol/L is abnormal and over 4 mmol/L is severe; failure to clear it predicts death.
Four families: hypovolemic, cardiogenic, obstructive, distributive — each with a different preload and resistance pattern.
Neurogenic shock is the one type with hypotension plus bradycardia and warm dry skin.

checks.q: A 24-year-old after a motorcycle crash has a heart rate of 128, blood pressure 118/96, cool clammy skin, and anxiety. The best interpretation is:
choices: He is not in shock because his blood pressure is normal
He is in compensated shock; the narrow pulse pressure and tachycardia show sympathetic compensation
He has neurogenic shock
He is simply anxious from the crash
checks.why: A narrowing pulse pressure, tachycardia, and cool clammy skin are sympathetic compensation maintaining a normal systolic pressure. Young patients compensate until they crash suddenly. Neurogenic shock would give bradycardia and warm dry skin, and attributing this to anxiety ignores the perfusion findings.

checks.q: A patient with a large anterior myocardial infarction is hypotensive with crackles throughout both lungs and cold mottled skin. What is the mechanism, and what would a 2 L fluid bolus do?
choices: Cardiogenic shock; fluid would worsen pulmonary edema because the failing ventricle cannot handle more preload
Hypovolemic shock; fluid is the treatment of choice
Distributive shock; fluid would restore vascular tone
Obstructive shock; fluid would relieve the obstruction
checks.why: A failing pump already has high filling pressures backing up into the lungs, which is why there are crackles. Adding volume worsens pulmonary edema. Treatment is inotropic support and reperfusion of the infarct, not more preload.

checks.q: A patient with a C5 spinal cord injury has a blood pressure of 82/48, a heart rate of 52, and warm dry skin. This pattern indicates:
choices: Hypovolemic shock from occult bleeding
Cardiogenic shock
Neurogenic shock from loss of sympathetic outflow
Septic shock
checks.why: Cord injury above about T6 severs sympathetic outflow, so vessels dilate and the heart cannot mount a compensatory tachycardia, producing hypotension with bradycardia and warm dry skin. Hemorrhagic and cardiogenic shock both cause tachycardia with cold clammy skin, and sepsis usually brings fever and tachycardia.

lessons.title: Sepsis: when the response becomes the disease
lessons.body:
## The definition changed for a reason

Sepsis is not an overwhelming infection. It is **a dysregulated host response to infection that causes organ dysfunction**. The bacteria start it; the immune system does the damage. That distinction explains why a patient with a simple urinary infection can die and a patient with a huge abscess can walk around.

The Sepsis-3 definitions are:

- **Sepsis**: suspected infection plus organ dysfunction, measured as a rise of `2` or more points in the SOFA score, which grades six organ systems (lung, blood, liver, cardiovascular, brain, kidney).
- **Septic shock**: sepsis that still needs a vasopressor to keep mean arterial pressure at `65 mmHg` or higher after adequate fluids, with a lactate above `2 mmol/L`. Mortality is roughly `40%`.

The old SIRS criteria (temperature, heart rate, respiratory rate, white count) are still a useful screen but are too nonspecific to define sepsis; a marathon runner meets them.

## The mechanism, step by step

1. Bacterial fragments such as endotoxin trigger immune cells.
2. Those cells release a flood of cytokines: TNF-alpha, interleukin-1, interleukin-6. This is the cytokine storm.
3. Cytokines cause massive nitric oxide production, and nitric oxide relaxes vascular smooth muscle everywhere. Systemic vascular resistance collapses.
4. The same mediators make capillaries leaky, so plasma escapes into the interstitium. The patient becomes functionally hypovolemic even though nothing was lost externally.
5. Coagulation is activated at the same time. Microthrombi form in small vessels while clotting factors are consumed, which is why severe sepsis can cause both clotting and bleeding.
6. Oxygen cannot be extracted or used properly at the cell, so lactate rises even when delivery looks adequate.

> **Key:** Septic shock is warm and vasodilated early (bounding pulses, flushed skin, high cardiac output) and cold and vasoconstricted late once the heart itself is depressed. Warm skin does not rule out shock.

## Why lactate rises

Two reasons at once. Tissue is hypoperfused, so cells burn fuel anaerobically. And sepsis impairs the mitochondria and the enzyme that feeds pyruvate into aerobic metabolism, so lactate accumulates even in well-perfused tissue. A lactate above `4 mmol/L` marks severe illness, and the key measure is lactate clearance: a level that falls with treatment predicts survival, and one that does not predicts the opposite.

## Why the order of treatment is fluids, then norepinephrine

The tank is leaking and the vessels are dilated. Crystalloid at `30 mL/kg` refills the compartment first, because a vasopressor squeezing an empty tank raises pressure numbers while starving tissue. Once the tank is adequately filled and pressure is still low, norepinephrine restores the tone that nitric oxide destroyed. Target mean arterial pressure is `65 mmHg`, the pressure below which kidney and brain autoregulation fails.

## The clock

Every hour of delay in effective antibiotics after septic shock is recognized raises mortality by several percentage points, which is why the bundle is built around the first hour: draw lactate and blood cultures before antibiotics, give broad-spectrum antibiotics, start `30 mL/kg` of crystalloid for hypotension or lactate above `4`, add vasopressors for a mean arterial pressure under `65`, and repeat the lactate.

> **On shift:** Cultures before antibiotics, but never let culture collection delay the antibiotic. If access is hard, the antibiotic still goes in.

## Multiple organ dysfunction

Sustained inflammation, microthrombi, and hypoperfusion damage organs in a predictable order. The kidneys fail early, because they were sacrificed first by compensation. The gut lining breaks down and leaks bacteria back into the portal circulation, feeding the fire. The lungs develop acute respiratory distress syndrome as capillaries leak into alveoli. The liver stops clearing drugs and making clotting factors. The brain becomes encephalopathic. Once three or more organ systems fail, mortality climbs above `50%`.
keyPoints: Sepsis is infection plus organ dysfunction; the damage comes from the host response, not the bacteria.
Septic shock is a vasopressor requirement to hold MAP at 65 after fluids, plus lactate over 2 mmol/L.
Cytokines drive nitric oxide release (vasodilation) and capillary leak (functional hypovolemia) at the same time.
Fluids come first at 30 mL/kg, then norepinephrine; a pressor on an empty tank raises pressure but starves tissue.
Each hour of antibiotic delay in septic shock measurably increases mortality; lactate clearance predicts survival.

checks.q: Why does a septic patient become hypotensive even though no blood or fluid has been lost from the body?
choices: The heart stops contracting entirely
Cytokine-driven nitric oxide dilates vessels and leaky capillaries push plasma into the interstitium, producing relative and then real hypovolemia
Bacteria physically block the arteries
Antibiotics lower blood pressure
checks.why: Sepsis enlarges the container through vasodilation and simultaneously empties it through capillary leak, so the patient is both vasodilated and functionally hypovolemic. Cardiac output is typically high early, bacteria do not occlude arteries, and antibiotics are not the cause of the hypotension.

checks.q: A patient with pneumonia has a blood pressure of 84/50 after 30 mL/kg of crystalloid and a lactate of 4.6 mmol/L. This meets the definition of:
choices: Sepsis but not septic shock
SIRS only
Septic shock, because vasopressors are needed to keep MAP at 65 despite adequate fluids and lactate is above 2
Cardiogenic shock
checks.why: Septic shock is defined by persistent hypotension requiring vasopressors to maintain a MAP of 65 after adequate fluid resuscitation, together with a lactate above 2 mmol/L. Sepsis alone means organ dysfunction without that pressor requirement, and SIRS is only a screening construct.

checks.q: A septic patient's initial lactate is 5.2 mmol/L; after 3 hours of treatment it is 5.4 mmol/L. What does this indicate?
choices: Failure to clear lactate, a strong predictor of poor outcome that should prompt reassessment of source control and perfusion
The lab is likely in error since treatment was given
Normal variation that requires no action
It means the patient is no longer septic
checks.why: Lactate clearance is one of the best available prognostic markers in sepsis. A flat or rising lactate after resuscitation suggests ongoing hypoperfusion or an uncontrolled source such as an undrained abscess, and it demands reassessment rather than reassurance.

lessons.title: Arterial occlusion: heart attack and brain attack
lessons.body:
## The plaque story

Atherosclerosis begins with injury to the endothelium, the single layer of cells lining an artery, from high blood pressure, smoking, high glucose, or high LDL. LDL slips into the wall, gets oxidized, and macrophages eat it until they become foam cells. That fatty streak matures into a plaque with a lipid core under a fibrous cap.

The plaque that kills is not usually the biggest one. A **vulnerable plaque** has a thin cap, a large soft lipid core, and active inflammation eating at the cap from within. It may narrow the artery only `40%`, which is why a patient can have a normal stress test in March and an infarct in April.

When the cap tears, blood meets collagen and tissue factor. Platelets stick, activate, and recruit more platelets, and the coagulation cascade lays fibrin over the top. A thrombus forms in seconds to minutes.

## Supply versus demand

**Stable angina** is a demand problem: a fixed narrowing that supplies enough blood at rest but not during exertion. Predictable, brought on by effort, relieved by rest or nitroglycerin in minutes.

**Acute coronary syndrome** is a supply problem: a clot that suddenly cuts flow regardless of what the patient is doing. That is why it happens at rest and is not relieved by rest.

| Syndrome | Occlusion | Muscle | Troponin | ECG |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Unstable angina | partial, transient | ischemic, not dead | normal | may be normal or show depression |
| NSTEMI | partial or transient complete | inner layer dies | elevated | ST depression or T inversion, no elevation |
| STEMI | complete and persistent | full thickness dies | elevated | ST elevation, then Q waves |

## Troponin kinetics

Troponin leaks once myocyte membranes rupture. It becomes detectable in `2-4` hours with conventional assays and within `1-2` hours with high-sensitivity assays, peaks at `12-24` hours, and stays elevated `7-10` days. Because of that long tail, a single value cannot tell you when the injury happened, so two values `1-3` hours apart are compared. A rising or falling pattern, the **delta**, means acute injury. A flat elevated value usually means chronic damage from kidney disease, heart failure, pulmonary embolism, or sepsis.

> **Key:** Troponin says heart muscle died. It does not say why. Elevated troponin is not synonymous with heart attack.

## Why minutes matter

Myocardium becomes irreversibly injured after about `20-30` minutes of complete occlusion, and the infarct spreads outward from the inner layer over roughly `6` hours. That is the basis for a `90`-minute door-to-balloon target.

Complications follow a schedule. Ventricular fibrillation is most likely in the first hours and is the leading cause of prehospital death. Cardiogenic shock appears when more than about `40%` of the left ventricle is lost. Papillary muscle rupture causes sudden severe mitral regurgitation and flash pulmonary edema around days `3-5`. Free wall rupture causes tamponade and sudden death around days `3-7`. Pericarditis can appear early or weeks later.

## Stroke is the same story in a different artery

About `87%` of strokes are ischemic. **Thrombotic** strokes form on local atherosclerosis and often stutter or progress over minutes to hours. **Embolic** strokes arrive from elsewhere, most often a fibrillating left atrium that lets blood pool and clot, and produce a deficit that is maximal at onset.

About `13%` are hemorrhagic. Intracerebral hemorrhage is usually hypertensive bleeding into the deep structures. Subarachnoid hemorrhage is usually a ruptured berry aneurysm producing a thunderclap headache that peaks within seconds.

## The penumbra

An occluded cerebral artery creates a dead core surrounded by the **penumbra**: tissue that is not getting enough blood to function but is still alive, kept marginally perfused by collateral vessels. Restore flow and the penumbra recovers; wait and it joins the core. Roughly `1.9` million neurons die per minute of untreated large-vessel stroke.

A **transient ischemic attack** is a deficit that resolves without infarction. It is a warning with a high risk of completed stroke within `48` hours.

> **Trap:** Blood pressure in acute ischemic stroke is usually left high on purpose, because the penumbra depends on pressure to perfuse through collaterals. Treatment thresholds are roughly `220/120` normally, but `185/110` if thrombolytics are being given.
keyPoints: The plaque that ruptures is often only 40% stenotic; a thin cap and inflammation matter more than size.
Unstable angina has no troponin rise, NSTEMI kills the inner layer, STEMI kills full thickness.
Troponin rises in 2-4 hours, peaks at 12-24, and lasts 7-10 days, so the delta between two values defines acute injury.
Embolic strokes are maximal at onset, often from atrial fibrillation; thrombotic strokes stutter.
The penumbra is salvageable tissue kept alive by collaterals, which is why blood pressure is left high in ischemic stroke.

checks.q: A patient had a normal stress test 8 months ago and now has a STEMI. What best explains this?
choices: The stress test must have been misread
Plaques that rupture are often only modestly stenotic; a thin inflamed cap, not the degree of narrowing, predicts rupture
Coronary plaque can grow from 0% to 100% in 8 months
Stress tests only detect hemorrhagic events
checks.why: Stress testing detects flow-limiting stenoses, but the lesions that rupture and thrombose are frequently 40% to 60% narrowings with thin fibrous caps and active inflammation. A normal stress test therefore never excludes future plaque rupture.

checks.q: A patient with chronic kidney disease has a troponin of 0.09 ng/mL on arrival and 0.09 ng/mL three hours later, with no chest pain. This pattern suggests:
choices: Acute myocardial infarction requiring immediate catheterization
Laboratory error requiring a third sample
Chronic troponin elevation, since acute injury produces a rising or falling delta rather than a flat value
Unstable angina
checks.why: Acute myocardial injury produces a dynamic pattern because troponin is actively leaking and then clearing. A flat elevated level is typical of chronic myocardial strain in kidney disease or heart failure. Unstable angina by definition has no troponin elevation at all.

checks.q: Why is a blood pressure of 200/110 often left untreated in an acute ischemic stroke that is not receiving thrombolytics?
choices: Because lowering it would raise intracranial pressure
Because the ischemic penumbra depends on perfusion pressure through collateral vessels, and dropping pressure enlarges the infarct
Because antihypertensives do not work during a stroke
Because high blood pressure dissolves the clot
checks.why: Autoregulation is lost in ischemic brain, so penumbral perfusion becomes directly pressure-dependent and aggressive lowering converts salvageable tissue into infarct. Permissive hypertension is tolerated to roughly 220/120, tightened to 185/110 when thrombolytics are used.

lessons.title: Heart failure: forward failure and backward congestion
lessons.body:
## Two different failures with the same name

Heart failure means the heart cannot deliver enough blood for the body's needs at normal filling pressures. It comes in two mechanical flavors.

**Reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF)** is a squeeze problem. The ventricle is dilated and weak, ejecting under `40%` of its contents, usually after infarction, long-standing hypertension, valve disease, alcohol, or viral myocarditis.

**Preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF)** is a filling problem. The ventricle is thick and stiff, ejects a normal fraction of a small volume, and cannot relax to fill. It is the classic failure of the older hypertensive patient and now accounts for roughly half of all heart failure.

## Forward and backward

Every symptom sorts into two buckets.

**Forward failure** is not enough output ahead of the pump: fatigue, exercise intolerance, cool extremities, falling urine output, and in the extreme, confusion and cardiogenic shock.

**Backward congestion** is blood damming up behind the pump, and which side fails decides where it dams.

| Side that fails | Blood backs into | What you see |
|---|---|---|
| Left | lungs | shortness of breath, orthopnea, waking at night gasping, crackles, pink frothy sputum |
| Right | systemic veins | distended neck veins, enlarged tender liver, ascites, pitting leg edema |

The most common cause of right-sided failure is left-sided failure, because chronic pulmonary congestion raises the pressure the right ventricle must pump against. Right failure from lung disease alone has its own name, cor pulmonale.

**BNP** is a hormone released by stretched ventricular muscle, so it rises with filling pressure. Under `100 pg/mL` argues strongly against acute heart failure as the cause of breathlessness; above `400-500 pg/mL` supports it. Obesity falsely lowers it and kidney disease falsely raises it.

## The compensations that make it worse

The body reads low cardiac output as low blood volume and responds as though the patient were bleeding.

1. **Sympathetic activation** raises heart rate and contractility. That buys output now, but it raises myocardial oxygen demand and shortens diastole, which is when coronary arteries actually fill.
2. **Renin-angiotensin-aldosterone activation** constricts vessels and retains salt and water. That raises preload and afterload, so the failing ventricle now has more to pump and more resistance to pump against.
3. **Remodeling**: chronic angiotensin II and catecholamine exposure makes the ventricle dilate and fibrose, which weakens it further.

> **Key:** Every drug that improves survival in heart failure blocks a compensation rather than stimulating the heart. ACE inhibitors and ARBs block the RAAS arm, beta blockers block the sympathetic arm, and aldosterone antagonists block remodeling. Drugs that flog the heart harder relieve symptoms but shorten life.

## What tips a compensated patient over

The usual triggers are dietary salt, missed medications, a new arrhythmia (atrial fibrillation removes the atrial kick, which a stiff ventricle depends on), infection, ischemia, uncontrolled hypertension, anemia, and NSAIDs, which cause salt retention and blunt diuretics.

## Flash pulmonary edema

Sometimes it is not slow congestion. A sudden spike in afterload, usually a hypertensive crisis, makes a stiff ventricle unable to eject, and pressure transmits backward into the pulmonary capillaries within minutes. Plasma is forced into alveoli and the patient drowns in their own serum: severe breathlessness, sitting bolt upright, sweating, sometimes pink frothy sputum.

These patients are usually not overloaded with total body fluid; the fluid they have is in the wrong compartment. That is why the first treatments are noninvasive positive pressure ventilation, which pushes fluid back out of alveoli and reduces preload, and nitroglycerin, which drops preload and afterload in minutes. Diuresis matters, but it is not what saves the first ten minutes.

> **On shift:** A heart failure patient who cannot lie flat for a chest x-ray is telling you the diagnosis. Orthopnea quantified in pillows is a real measurement worth reporting.
keyPoints: HFrEF is a squeeze problem with EF under 40%; HFpEF is a stiff ventricle that cannot fill with a normal EF.
Left failure backs up into lungs (orthopnea, crackles); right failure backs up into the body (JVD, edema, ascites).
The most common cause of right heart failure is left heart failure.
BNP under 100 pg/mL argues against acute heart failure; obesity lowers it and kidney disease raises it.
Sympathetic and RAAS compensation worsen failure, which is why survival drugs block them rather than stimulate the heart.

checks.q: A patient has distended neck veins, a tender enlarged liver, and pitting edema to the thighs, with clear lungs. This pattern indicates:
choices: Left-sided heart failure
Right-sided heart failure, with blood backing up into the systemic veins
Acute pulmonary embolism only
Hypovolemic shock
checks.why: Right ventricular failure dams blood into the systemic venous system, producing jugular distension, hepatic congestion, ascites, and dependent edema, while the lungs stay clear. Left-sided failure produces pulmonary congestion instead, and hypovolemia would give flat neck veins.

checks.q: Why do ACE inhibitors improve survival in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction?
choices: They increase the force of contraction directly
They raise heart rate to improve output
They block the RAAS compensation that raises preload and afterload and drives remodeling
They dissolve coronary plaque
checks.why: Angiotensin II and aldosterone worsen failure by constricting vessels, retaining salt and water, and promoting fibrosis and dilation. Blocking that loop improves survival, whereas inotropes that stimulate the heart relieve symptoms but increase mortality.

checks.q: A hypertensive patient develops severe breathlessness over 20 minutes with a blood pressure of 218/120 and pink frothy sputum. The mechanism is:
choices: Total body fluid overload requiring large-volume diuresis as the first step
A sudden afterload spike preventing ejection, driving pressure backward into pulmonary capillaries and flooding alveoli
Pneumonia with consolidation
Bronchospasm from undiagnosed asthma
checks.why: Flash pulmonary edema is a redistribution problem, not usually a total volume problem: the afterload spike stops a stiff ventricle from ejecting and pressure transmits back into the lungs within minutes. Positive pressure ventilation and nitroglycerin address it fastest, with diuresis secondary.

lessons.title: Respiratory failure: oxygen in, carbon dioxide out
lessons.body:
## Two failures, two gases

**Type 1, hypoxemic failure**, is an oxygenation problem: PaO2 below `60 mmHg` on room air. The lung cannot get oxygen into blood.

**Type 2, hypercapnic failure**, is a ventilation problem: PaCO2 above `45 mmHg`. The bellows cannot move enough air, either because the patient will not breathe (opioids, brain injury), cannot breathe (neuromuscular weakness, exhaustion), or cannot move air through obstructed airways.

Hypoxemia has five causes, and the useful one is **V/Q mismatch**: some alveoli get air without blood, others get blood without air. Its extreme form is **shunt**, where blood passes completely unventilated alveoli. Shunt is the one that does not improve much with supplemental oxygen, because the blood never meets the oxygen you are giving.

## ARDS

Acute respiratory distress syndrome is a leaky-membrane disease. Systemic inflammation, usually from sepsis, pancreatitis, aspiration, or trauma, damages the alveolar-capillary membrane. Protein-rich fluid pours into alveoli, surfactant is diluted and destroyed, and alveoli collapse. The result is a massive shunt with stiff lungs.

It is defined by onset within one week of an insult, bilateral infiltrates not explained by heart failure, and a PaO2 to FiO2 ratio of `300` or less. The treatment that changed mortality is mechanical: low tidal volumes of about `6 mL/kg` of predicted body weight, because large breaths tear the few open alveoli that remain.

## Pulmonary embolism

A clot, usually from a leg vein, lodges in the pulmonary circulation. Those alveoli are ventilated but not perfused, creating **dead space** and V/Q mismatch. The patient breathes fast, blows off carbon dioxide, and typically shows a respiratory alkalosis with hypoxemia and a clear chest x-ray.

A large embolism is a circulatory problem more than a gas problem. Blocked outflow raises right ventricular afterload abruptly, the thin right ventricle dilates and fails, the septum bows into the left ventricle, and the left side cannot fill. That is obstructive shock, and it is how pulmonary embolism kills.

## Asthma versus COPD

**Asthma** is reversible: bronchial smooth muscle constricts, the mucosa swells, and mucus plugs the airway, all driven by inflammation. Airflow out is limited, so air stacks up behind closed airways and expiration is prolonged.

> **Trap:** In a severe attack, a quiet chest is worse than loud wheezing, because wheeze requires moving air. A PaCO2 that rises from low to normal in a tiring asthmatic means the patient is failing, not improving.

**COPD** is destruction. Emphysema destroys alveolar walls and the elastic recoil that normally pulls airways open, so airways collapse on exhalation and air is trapped. Chronic bronchitis adds mucus and inflammation. Carbon dioxide climbs chronically and the kidney compensates by retaining bicarbonate, which is why a COPD patient can live at a PaCO2 of `55 mmHg` with a near-normal pH. Oxygen is targeted to a saturation of `88-92%` rather than higher, because excess oxygen worsens V/Q matching and can raise carbon dioxide further.

## Pneumonia and pneumothorax

**Pneumonia** fills alveoli with inflammatory fluid and pus. Consolidated lung is perfused but not ventilated, which is a shunt; that is why a lobar pneumonia can make a patient profoundly hypoxemic.

**Pneumothorax** is air in the pleural space, which destroys the negative pressure that holds the lung expanded, so the lung collapses. A **simple** pneumothorax is stable. An **open** one communicates with the outside through a chest wall wound. A **tension** pneumothorax has a one-way valve: air enters with each breath and cannot escape, pressure rises, the mediastinum shifts, and the vena cava kinks so blood cannot return to the heart. That is obstructive shock with distended neck veins, a tracheal shift away from the affected side, and absent breath sounds, and it is treated on clinical findings with immediate needle decompression, not after a chest x-ray.
keyPoints: Type 1 failure is hypoxemia (PaO2 under 60); type 2 is hypercapnia (PaCO2 over 45) from pump failure.
Shunt is the form of V/Q mismatch that does not correct with supplemental oxygen.
ARDS is a leaky alveolar membrane with bilateral infiltrates and a P/F ratio of 300 or less, treated with 6 mL/kg tidal volumes.
A large pulmonary embolism kills through right ventricular failure and obstructive shock, not hypoxemia alone.
A silent chest in asthma and a normalizing PaCO2 in a tiring asthmatic are pre-arrest findings.

checks.q: A patient with lobar pneumonia has a saturation of 84% that barely improves on a non-rebreather. The physiologic reason is:
choices: Shunt: blood flows past consolidated alveoli that contain no air, so it never contacts the oxygen you are delivering
Hypoventilation from pain
Carbon monoxide poisoning
The pulse oximeter cannot read in pneumonia
checks.why: Consolidated lung is perfused but not ventilated, the definition of shunt, and shunted blood mixes back into the arterial circulation unchanged no matter how much oxygen is supplied. Hypoventilation would raise carbon dioxide and respond well to oxygen.

checks.q: An asthmatic in severe distress for 40 minutes now has a quiet chest and a PaCO2 that rose from 28 to 41 mmHg. This means:
choices: He is improving, since wheezing has stopped and carbon dioxide has normalized
He is tiring and approaching respiratory arrest; a quiet chest means air is no longer moving
He has developed pneumonia
The blood gas was drawn incorrectly
checks.why: Wheeze requires airflow, so its disappearance in a still-distressed patient signals critically low air movement. A tiring asthmatic's PaCO2 rises from low toward normal as ventilation fails, so a normal value in this context is ominous rather than reassuring.

checks.q: A trauma patient becomes hypotensive with distended neck veins, absent breath sounds on the right, and tracheal deviation to the left. The mechanism of the shock is:
choices: Hypovolemia from blood loss into the chest
Cardiogenic shock from myocardial contusion
Obstructive shock, because rising pleural pressure kinks the vena cava and prevents venous return
Neurogenic shock from a thoracic spine injury
checks.why: A tension pneumothorax raises intrapleural pressure until the mediastinum shifts and venous return is mechanically obstructed, which is obstructive shock. Distended neck veins argue against hypovolemia, and the treatment is immediate needle decompression on clinical grounds.

lessons.title: Diabetic emergencies and reading acid-base
lessons.body:
## Diabetic ketoacidosis, step by step

1. **No insulin.** Glucose cannot enter cells, so despite a bloodstream full of sugar the cells are starving.
2. **Counterregulatory hormones rise.** Glucagon, cortisol, catecholamines, and growth hormone all push the liver to make more glucose, which makes the hyperglycemia worse.
3. **Fat is broken down.** Lipolysis floods the liver with free fatty acids, which it converts to ketoacids: beta-hydroxybutyrate and acetoacetate. Acetone is the volatile byproduct, and it is what you smell.
4. **Acidosis.** Ketoacids consume bicarbonate and create an anion gap metabolic acidosis. The lungs compensate with deep rapid Kussmaul respirations to blow off carbon dioxide.
5. **Osmotic diuresis.** Above a serum glucose of roughly `180 mg/dL` the kidney cannot reabsorb it all, and glucose in the urine drags water with it. The patient urinates out liters along with sodium, potassium, magnesium, and phosphate.
6. **Dehydration and shock.** Typical fluid deficits run `5-8 L`.

> **Key:** The potassium trap. Acidosis and insulin deficiency push potassium out of cells, so the serum potassium reads normal or high while total body potassium is severely depleted. Give insulin and potassium rushes back into cells, and the number falls fast. Potassium below about `3.3 mEq/L` must be replaced before insulin starts.

## Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state

HHS is the type 2 version. Enough insulin remains to suppress ketone production but not nearly enough to control glucose. Without ketoacidosis there is no early warning, so it builds over days to weeks: glucose often above `600 mg/dL`, serum osmolality above `320 mOsm/kg`, extreme dehydration, and progressive confusion or coma. There is minimal acidosis and no fruity breath. Mortality is higher than DKA, roughly `10-20%`, because the patients are older and more dehydrated by the time they present.

## Hypoglycemia

The brain burns glucose almost exclusively and stores none. Below about `70 mg/dL`, adrenaline symptoms appear: tremor, sweating, palpitations, hunger, anxiety. Below about `50 mg/dL` the brain itself starves, producing confusion, slurred speech, focal deficits that mimic stroke, seizures, and coma.

Two traps: beta blockers blunt the adrenaline warning, so the first sign may be collapse; and sulfonylurea-induced hypoglycemia recurs for many hours after the patient is fed and looks better.

## Reading an acid-base panel

Normals: pH `7.35-7.45`, PaCO2 `35-45 mmHg`, bicarbonate `22-26 mEq/L`.

1. Look at the pH. Below `7.35` is acidemia, above `7.45` is alkalemia.
2. Ask which value explains it. A high PaCO2 with low pH is respiratory acidosis; a low bicarbonate with low pH is metabolic acidosis.
3. For a metabolic acidosis, calculate the anion gap: sodium minus the sum of chloride and bicarbonate, normal `8-12`.

**Anion gap acidosis** means an acid was added. Remember MUDPILES: methanol, uremia, diabetic ketoacidosis, propylene glycol, isoniazid, lactic acidosis, ethylene glycol, salicylates.

**Non-gap acidosis** means bicarbonate was lost or chloride gained: diarrhea, renal tubular acidosis, and large-volume normal saline.

| Disorder | pH | Primary change | Common cause |
|---|---|---|---|
| Metabolic acidosis | low | bicarbonate falls | DKA, lactic acidosis, diarrhea, kidney failure |
| Metabolic alkalosis | high | bicarbonate rises | vomiting, nasogastric suction, diuretics |
| Respiratory acidosis | low | PaCO2 rises | opioids, COPD, fatigue, chest wall injury |
| Respiratory alkalosis | high | PaCO2 falls | pain, anxiety, sepsis, pulmonary embolism, early salicylate poisoning |

Mixed pictures are common and informative. Aspirin overdose classically produces a respiratory alkalosis from direct stimulation of the brainstem plus an anion gap metabolic acidosis. A vomiting DKA patient has both a gap acidosis from ketones and an alkalosis from lost gastric acid, which can make the pH look deceptively normal.
keyPoints: DKA: no insulin, cells starve, fat is burned to ketoacids, glucose spills into urine and drags out liters of water.
Serum potassium reads high in DKA while total body potassium is depleted; insulin drives it back in and crashes the level.
HHS has enough insulin to block ketosis but not hyperglycemia: glucose over 600, osmolality over 320, higher mortality.
Below 50 mg/dL the brain starves and hypoglycemia mimics stroke; beta blockers hide the adrenaline warning signs.
Anion gap equals sodium minus chloride plus bicarbonate, normal 8-12; a raised gap means added acid (MUDPILES).

checks.q: In DKA, why does the serum potassium often read 5.4 mEq/L when the patient is actually potassium-depleted?
choices: The kidney retains potassium in acidosis
Acidosis and insulin deficiency shift potassium out of cells into the blood, while osmotic diuresis has already flushed the body's stores out in the urine
Ketones interfere with the assay
Dehydration always raises potassium
checks.why: Potassium leaves cells in acidosis and in the absence of insulin, so the measured serum value looks adequate while total body stores have been urinated away. This is why starting insulin without checking potassium can precipitate lethal hypokalemia.

checks.q: An arterial blood gas shows pH 7.22, PaCO2 26 mmHg, bicarbonate 11 mEq/L, with sodium 138, chloride 98. What is the disorder?
choices: Respiratory acidosis with metabolic compensation
Metabolic alkalosis
Anion gap metabolic acidosis with respiratory compensation
Respiratory alkalosis
checks.why: The pH is acidemic and the bicarbonate is low, which makes it metabolic acidosis; the low PaCO2 is appropriate respiratory compensation. The anion gap is 138 minus 109, which is 29, well above the normal 8-12, so an acid such as ketones or lactate has been added.

checks.q: How does hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state differ mechanistically from DKA?
choices: HHS patients have enough residual insulin to suppress ketone production but not hyperglycemia, so they present later and more dehydrated
HHS involves more ketones than DKA
HHS occurs only in type 1 diabetes
HHS has lower glucose levels than DKA
checks.why: A small amount of circulating insulin is enough to block lipolysis and ketogenesis while failing to control glucose, so HHS develops silently over days with glucose often above 600 mg/dL and osmolality above 320. It occurs in type 2 diabetes and carries higher mortality than DKA.

lessons.title: Kidney injury, rhabdomyolysis, and electrolyte emergencies
lessons.body:
## Acute kidney injury has three addresses

Acute kidney injury is an abrupt fall in filtration, defined as a creatinine rise of `0.3 mg/dL` within `48` hours, a rise to `1.5` times baseline, or urine output under `0.5 mL/kg/h` for `6` hours. Locate the problem before, inside, or after the kidney.

**Pre-renal** is underperfusion and it is the most common. Hypovolemia, hemorrhage, heart failure, sepsis, or the drug trio of an NSAID, an ACE inhibitor, and a diuretic. The tubules are healthy and desperate, so they reabsorb everything they can: BUN to creatinine ratio above `20:1`, fractional excretion of sodium under `1%`, concentrated urine, and clean sediment. Restore perfusion early and it reverses completely.

**Intrinsic** means the kidney tissue itself is damaged. Acute tubular necrosis is the usual form, caused by prolonged ischemia or by toxins: contrast, aminoglycosides, vancomycin, and myoglobin. The urine shows muddy brown granular casts, the fractional excretion of sodium rises above `2%`, and the kidney can no longer concentrate. Interstitial nephritis is a drug allergy inside the kidney; glomerulonephritis shows red cell casts.

**Post-renal** is obstruction: an enlarged prostate, a stone blocking a solitary kidney or both ureters, tumor, or clot. A bladder scan and an ultrasound find it, and relieving it quickly is curative.

When filtration fails, waste accumulates. **Uremia** produces nausea, loss of appetite, confusion with asterixis, itching, bleeding from platelet dysfunction, and pericarditis with a friction rub. Emergent dialysis is driven by five things, remembered as AEIOU: severe acidosis, electrolytes meaning refractory hyperkalemia, intoxications, fluid overload, and uremic pericarditis or encephalopathy.

## Rhabdomyolysis

Skeletal muscle breaks down and dumps its contents into the blood after crush injury, a long down time on a hard floor, prolonged seizures, extreme exertion, stimulant use, or a statin interaction. Creatine kinase above `5,000 units/L` is significant and above `20,000` carries high renal risk.

Three things happen at once. Myoglobin precipitates in and obstructs tubules and is directly toxic to them. Potassium and phosphate flood out of dying muscle, so hyperkalemia is the early killer. Calcium moves into the injured muscle, so patients are hypocalcemic early and may become hypercalcemic later as it releases. Treatment is aggressive volume to keep the tubules flushed.

## Hyperkalemia

Potassium sets the resting membrane potential. As it rises, the resting potential becomes less negative and the cell is initially more excitable, then sodium channels inactivate and conduction slows and fails.

| Potassium | ECG |
|---|---|
| `5.5-6.5 mEq/L` | tall peaked T waves |
| `6.5-7.5 mEq/L` | flattened P waves, prolonged PR |
| `7-8 mEq/L` | widened QRS |
| above `8 mEq/L` | sine wave, then arrest |

> **Key:** Treatment has three separate jobs in order. Calcium stabilizes the cardiac membrane within minutes and does not lower potassium at all. Insulin with glucose, albuterol, and bicarbonate shift potassium into cells temporarily. Only diuretics, binders, and dialysis actually remove it. Skipping to a shift without giving calcium leaves the heart unprotected.

## Hyponatremia

Sodium is a water problem, not a salt problem. Excess free water dilutes the blood, so water moves down its osmotic gradient into brain cells and the brain swells inside a fixed skull: headache, nausea, confusion, then seizures below roughly `120 mEq/L`.

The brain adapts over days by pushing solutes out. Correct a chronic low sodium too quickly and water is yanked out of those adapted neurons, destroying myelin in the pons. Osmotic demyelination appears days later as a locked-in patient, and it is permanent. Correction is limited to about `6-8 mEq/L` in `24` hours, with `100 mL` boluses of `3%` saline reserved for active seizures.

## Calcium

**High calcium** comes mostly from hyperparathyroidism and malignancy, and produces stones, bone pain, abdominal groans, and psychiatric overtones, with a short QT. Volume is the treatment.

**Low calcium** causes tetany, tingling around the mouth, facial twitching when the cheek is tapped, carpal spasm with a blood pressure cuff, laryngospasm, and a prolonged QT. Think kidney failure, pancreatitis, massive transfusion with citrate, and neck surgery.
keyPoints: Pre-renal AKI shows BUN:Cr above 20:1 and FENa under 1%; acute tubular necrosis shows muddy brown casts and FENa above 2%.
Emergent dialysis indications: acidosis, electrolytes, intoxication, overload, uremia (AEIOU).
Rhabdomyolysis kills early through hyperkalemia and late through myoglobin-induced tubular injury; CK over 5,000 is significant.
Hyperkalemia ECG progression: peaked T waves, then flat P and long PR, then wide QRS, then sine wave.
Correct sodium no faster than 6-8 mEq/L in 24 hours or risk permanent osmotic demyelination.

checks.q: A dehydrated patient has a creatinine of 2.2 mg/dL, a BUN of 58 mg/dL, a FENa of 0.4%, and no casts. The most likely mechanism is:
choices: Pre-renal azotemia, with intact tubules avidly reabsorbing sodium and water
Acute tubular necrosis
Obstruction from an enlarged prostate
Acute interstitial nephritis
checks.why: A BUN to creatinine ratio above 20:1 with a fractional excretion of sodium under 1% and bland urine means healthy tubules responding to underperfusion by conserving sodium. Acute tubular necrosis loses that ability, giving FENa above 2% and muddy brown granular casts.

checks.q: A dialysis patient has a potassium of 7.6 mEq/L with a widened QRS. What is given first and why?
choices: Insulin with dextrose, because it lowers potassium fastest
Sodium polystyrene, because it removes potassium from the body
Calcium gluconate, because it stabilizes the cardiac membrane within minutes even though it does not lower potassium
Furosemide, because it increases urinary potassium loss
checks.why: With ECG changes the immediate threat is arrhythmia, and calcium raises the threshold for depolarization within minutes, buying time. Insulin and albuterol shift potassium intracellularly afterward, and binders or dialysis are what actually remove it; a dialysis patient makes little urine so furosemide is ineffective.

checks.q: A patient with a chronic sodium of 112 mEq/L is corrected to 132 mEq/L over 18 hours and days later becomes quadriparetic and unable to speak. This complication is:
choices: Cerebral edema from undercorrection
Osmotic demyelination syndrome from correcting too rapidly
A new ischemic stroke unrelated to treatment
Hypokalemic paralysis
checks.why: A 20 mEq/L rise in 18 hours far exceeds the 6-8 mEq/L per 24 hours limit. The chronically adapted brain loses water abruptly and pontine myelin is destroyed, producing a delayed, usually permanent locked-in picture. Cerebral edema is the danger of the low sodium itself, not of overcorrection.

lessons.title: The acute abdomen and the failure to clot
lessons.body:
## Appendicitis is a plumbing problem

Something blocks the appendiceal lumen, usually a hardened stool pellet or swollen lymphoid tissue. Mucus keeps being secreted behind the blockage, so pressure rises. That stretch is sensed by visceral nerves that cannot localize, which is why the pain starts vague and periumbilical. Rising pressure then chokes off venous drainage, the wall becomes ischemic, gut bacteria invade, and the inflamed surface finally touches the parietal peritoneum of the abdominal wall, which is precisely mapped. That is the moment the pain migrates to the right lower quadrant and becomes sharp. Untreated, the wall perforates in `24-72` hours.

> **Key:** Visceral pain is dull, central, and hard to point to. Parietal pain is sharp, localized, and worse with movement. Pain that migrates from one to the other is the signature of an inflamed organ reaching the abdominal wall.

## The biliary ladder

Gallstones cause four different diseases depending on where the stone sits and whether infection joins in.

1. **Biliary colic**: a stone temporarily blocks the cystic duct during contraction after a fatty meal. Pain for minutes to hours, then it passes.
2. **Cholecystitis**: the blockage persists, the gallbladder wall becomes inflamed and infected. Constant right upper quadrant pain, fever, and arrest of inspiration on palpation.
3. **Choledocholithiasis**: a stone lodges in the common bile duct, so bile cannot reach the intestine. Jaundice, dark urine, rising bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase.
4. **Cholangitis**: that obstructed duct becomes infected, and pressure drives bacteria into the bloodstream. Charcot's triad is fever, jaundice, and right upper quadrant pain; add hypotension and confusion and it is Reynolds' pentad. This one needs drainage now.

## Pancreatitis, obstruction, and ischemia

**Pancreatitis** is the organ digesting itself. Trypsin activates prematurely inside the pancreas instead of in the duodenum and sets off every other enzyme. Gallstones and alcohol cause `70-80%` of cases. The inflamed gland leaks fluid into the retroperitoneum, so patients third-space liters and can become hypovolemic, develop ARDS, and drop their calcium as it binds to digested fat.

**Bowel obstruction** from adhesions, hernia, or tumor causes proximal distension, vomiting, and sequestration of liters of fluid into the gut lumen, which is why these patients are dry. If the blood supply is compromised, the bowel strangulates: fever, tachycardia, peritonitis, and rising lactate mean it is dying.

**Mesenteric ischemia** is an embolus or thrombus in the mesenteric circulation. The hallmark is severe pain with a soft, unremarkable abdomen, because the gut is ischemic but not yet inflamed. By the time the abdomen is rigid and lactate is high, bowel is dead. Pain out of proportion to examination in an older patient with atrial fibrillation is the pattern.

**GI bleeding** above the ligament of Treitz produces vomited blood and black tarry stool, and the digested blood raises the BUN. Below it produces red blood per rectum. Either can cause hemorrhagic shock, and the hemoglobin is often normal early because whole blood is lost, so the concentration does not change until fluid shifts in.

**Hepatic failure** costs three functions at once: synthesis (low albumin, high INR from missing clotting factors), detoxification (ammonia rises and causes encephalopathy), and normal portal flow (varices, ascites, splenomegaly).

## When clotting fails

Hemostasis has two stages: platelets plug the hole with help from von Willebrand factor, then the coagulation cascade lays down fibrin to reinforce it.

| Disorder | Defect | Pattern |
|---|---|---|
| Hemophilia A or B | factor VIII or IX missing | deep bleeds into joints and muscle, prolonged PTT, normal platelets |
| von Willebrand disease | platelet adhesion fails | nosebleeds, gum bleeding, heavy periods, easy bruising |
| Thrombocytopenia | too few platelets | petechiae and mucosal bleeding, spontaneous risk below `20,000` |
| Disseminated intravascular coagulation | cascade activated everywhere | clotting and bleeding at once: low platelets, low fibrinogen, high D-dimer, prolonged PT and PTT |

DIC is consumption. Sepsis, trauma, obstetric catastrophe, or cancer triggers widespread clotting that uses up platelets and factors, so the patient throws microthrombi that damage organs while oozing from every puncture site. Treating the trigger is the only definitive therapy.

> **On shift:** For any patient on warfarin or a DOAC, the same fall that bruises someone else can bleed into the head. Anticoagulation converts minor trauma into a time-critical scan.
keyPoints: Appendicitis pain migrates from vague periumbilical (visceral stretch) to sharp right lower quadrant (parietal irritation).
Charcot's triad of fever, jaundice, and right upper quadrant pain means cholangitis and needs urgent drainage.
Mesenteric ischemia presents as severe pain with a soft abdomen; a rigid abdomen means bowel is already dead.
Hemoglobin is often normal early in acute hemorrhage because whole blood is lost proportionally.
DIC consumes platelets and clotting factors, producing microthrombi and bleeding at the same time.

checks.q: Why does appendicitis pain typically begin around the umbilicus and later move to the right lower quadrant?
choices: The appendix physically migrates during inflammation
Early distension stimulates poorly localizing visceral nerves; later, inflammation contacts the precisely mapped parietal peritoneum
The pain is referred from the gallbladder first
Early pain is psychological and later pain is real
checks.why: Visceral afferents from a distended hollow organ produce dull, midline, poorly localized pain. Once the inflamed serosa touches the somatically innervated parietal peritoneum, the pain becomes sharp and precisely located over the appendix.

checks.q: An 78-year-old with atrial fibrillation has 10 out of 10 abdominal pain for 2 hours but a soft, minimally tender abdomen and a lactate of 2.1 mmol/L. The most concerning diagnosis is:
choices: Gastroenteritis
Constipation
Acute mesenteric ischemia, where pain out of proportion to examination precedes infarction and peritonitis
Musculoskeletal strain
checks.why: An embolic source plus severe pain with an unimpressive abdomen is the classic early window of mesenteric ischemia, before the bowel dies and inflames the peritoneum. Waiting for a rigid abdomen and a high lactate means waiting for infarcted bowel.

checks.q: A septic patient develops oozing from every IV site with platelets of 42,000, fibrinogen of 90 mg/dL, a markedly elevated D-dimer, and prolonged PT and PTT. This is:
choices: Hemophilia A
Disseminated intravascular coagulation from consumption of platelets and clotting factors
Warfarin overdose
von Willebrand disease
checks.why: Widespread cascade activation consumes platelets and factors, lowering fibrinogen and prolonging both PT and PTT while fibrin breakdown raises D-dimer. Hemophilia prolongs only the PTT with normal platelets, and warfarin prolongs PT without consuming fibrinogen or platelets.

lessons.title: Cancer, pain, and how to store a disease
lessons.body:
## What makes a cell malignant

A normal cell divides when told to and dies on schedule. A malignant cell has broken both rules. Growth-promoting genes get stuck on, tumor suppressor genes such as `p53` get switched off, the cell evades apoptosis, and it reactivates telomerase so it can divide without limit. Then it recruits its own blood supply through angiogenesis.

The step that makes cancer lethal is **invasion**: the tumor breaks through the basement membrane that normally confines it. From there it metastasizes, through lymphatics to regional nodes, through blood to lung, liver, bone, and brain, or by seeding across a body cavity. A benign tumor can grow large but stays encapsulated and does not invade.

Tumors kill by mass effect (blocking an airway, a bowel, a ureter, or compressing the spinal cord), by metabolic derangement, by crowding out bone marrow, by wasting (cachexia), and by making blood hypercoagulable.

## The oncologic emergencies

| Emergency | Mechanism | Clue |
|---|---|---|
| Tumor lysis syndrome | cells burst after chemotherapy and dump their contents | high potassium, phosphate, and uric acid, low calcium, kidney failure |
| Spinal cord compression | metastasis in a vertebra presses the cord | back pain plus weakness, numbness, or retention; give steroids and image now |
| Superior vena cava syndrome | tumor compresses the SVC | swelling of face and arms, distended chest veins, worse lying flat |
| Neutropenic fever | chemotherapy wiped out neutrophils | a single temperature of `38.3 C` with an absolute neutrophil count under `500`; antibiotics within `1` hour |
| Hypercalcemia of malignancy | tumor drives bone breakdown | confusion, constipation, dehydration, short QT |
| Hyperviscosity | too many cells or proteins thicken blood | blurred vision, headache, bleeding, confusion |

> **Trap:** New back pain in a cancer patient is spinal cord compression until proven otherwise. Once weakness appears, the window to preserve walking is measured in hours.

## How pain actually works

Pain is built in four steps.

1. **Transduction**: tissue damage releases prostaglandins, bradykinin, and hydrogen ions that open nociceptor channels and create an electrical signal. NSAIDs and local anesthetics work here.
2. **Transmission**: fast myelinated A-delta fibers carry sharp, immediate pain; slow unmyelinated C fibers carry the dull ache that follows. Both synapse in the dorsal horn of the spinal cord and ascend the spinothalamic tract.
3. **Modulation**: descending pathways from the brainstem release endorphins and dampen the dorsal horn signal. Opioids work largely here and in the brain.
4. **Perception**: the cortex assembles it into the experience of pain, shaped by attention, fear, and memory.

**Nociceptive** pain comes from real tissue damage: somatic pain is sharp and localized, visceral pain is dull and diffuse. **Neuropathic** pain comes from damaged nerve tissue itself, feels burning, shooting, or electric, and responds poorly to opioids and better to gabapentinoids and antidepressants.

**Referred pain** happens because visceral and skin nerves converge on the same spinal segment, and the brain misattributes the signal to the skin it knows better. Diaphragm irritation at C3 through C5 is felt in the shoulder. Cardiac afferents at T1 through T4 are felt in the jaw, neck, and left arm. Gallbladder pain is felt at the right scapula.

Pain that persists rewires the system: the dorsal horn becomes sensitized so normal input hurts more (hyperalgesia), and continuous opioid exposure downregulates receptors so the same dose does less.

## Storing diseases as illness scripts

Facts learned as lists disappear. Facts learned as scripts stay retrievable, because a script matches the shape of a real patient. Store every disease in the same five slots.

1. **Epidemiology**: who gets it, and what risk factors raise the odds.
2. **Pathophysiology**: the mechanism in one or two sentences.
3. **Presentation**: the symptoms and signs, and the ones that discriminate it from the near misses.
4. **Workup**: the test that confirms it and what that test shows.
5. **Treatment**: the first action and the definitive one.

Done for pulmonary embolism: young woman on estrogen after a long flight; clot from a leg vein blocks pulmonary arteries, creating dead space and raising right ventricular afterload; sudden pleuritic pain, breathlessness, tachycardia, clear lungs; CT pulmonary angiography confirms; anticoagulate, and thrombolyse if the right ventricle is failing.
keyPoints: Malignancy requires escaping growth control and apoptosis, then invading through the basement membrane and metastasizing.
New back pain in a cancer patient is spinal cord compression until proven otherwise; act before weakness appears.
Neutropenic fever is one temperature of 38.3 C with ANC under 500 and needs antibiotics within an hour.
Pain has four steps: transduction, transmission, modulation, perception — and each has its own drug class.
Referred pain happens because visceral and somatic nerves converge on the same spinal segment.

checks.q: A patient on chemotherapy for leukemia develops potassium 6.4 mEq/L, phosphate 8.2 mg/dL, uric acid 13 mg/dL, calcium 6.8 mg/dL, and a rising creatinine two days after treatment. This is:
choices: Tumor lysis syndrome from mass release of intracellular contents
Hypercalcemia of malignancy
Superior vena cava syndrome
Neutropenic fever
checks.why: Dying tumor cells dump potassium, phosphate, and nucleic acids that become uric acid; phosphate then binds calcium, lowering it, and urate crystals injure the kidney. Hypercalcemia of malignancy raises rather than lowers calcium, and the other two syndromes have entirely different findings.

checks.q: Why is gallbladder pain often felt at the right shoulder blade?
choices: Gallstones physically migrate toward the back
The gallbladder is anatomically located behind the scapula
Visceral afferents converge with somatic afferents at the same spinal segment, so the brain misattributes the signal to skin it maps better
Referred pain is caused by muscle spasm in the back
checks.why: Visceral pain fibers enter the cord at the same level as somatic fibers from a specific dermatome, and because the brain receives far more input from skin it assigns the sensation there. This is the same mechanism that sends cardiac pain to the jaw and arm and diaphragmatic irritation to the shoulder.

checks.q: A patient with known lung cancer reports new mid-back pain and today cannot feel his legs properly. The correct priority is:
choices: Discharge with analgesia and outpatient imaging
Treat as possible spinal cord compression with steroids and urgent imaging, because neurologic function lost is often not recovered
Order physical therapy for muscular back pain
Wait for the fever curve before imaging
checks.why: Metastatic cord compression progresses from pain to weakness to paralysis and incontinence, and function present at the time of treatment is roughly the function preserved. Delay costs ambulation permanently, so steroids and imaging happen immediately.

cards.front: Name the five cellular adaptations and give an example of each.
cards.back: Hypertrophy (thickened left ventricle), hyperplasia (enlarged prostate), atrophy (limb in a cast), metaplasia (Barrett esophagus), dysplasia (disordered precancerous cells).

cards.front: At what point does cell injury become irreversible?
cards.back: When membranes rupture: calcium floods the cytoplasm, lysosomes spill enzymes, and mitochondria are destroyed. Before that, ATP failure and swelling are fully reversible if perfusion returns.

cards.front: Why do lab tests like troponin, lipase, and ALT indicate organ damage?
cards.back: Each is a protein that normally stays inside a cell. Finding it in blood means cell membranes ruptured and the contents leaked out.

cards.front: Distinguish hypoxia, ischemia, and infarction.
cards.back: Hypoxia is low oxygen with flow intact. Ischemia is loss of flow, so oxygen and glucose stop and acid accumulates. Infarction is the resulting tissue death.

cards.front: How long do brain, heart, and skeletal muscle survive complete ischemia?
cards.back: Brain neurons 4-6 minutes, heart muscle irreversibly injured by 20-30 minutes and largely dead by 6 hours, skeletal muscle 4-6 hours.

cards.front: Contrast necrosis and apoptosis.
cards.back: Necrosis: uncontrolled, the cell swells and bursts, contents spill, inflammation follows. Apoptosis: programmed and energy-requiring, the cell shrinks and is packaged away with no inflammation.

cards.front: What are the five cardinal signs of acute inflammation and the first cell to arrive?
cards.back: Redness, heat, swelling, pain, and loss of function, from vasodilation and increased permeability. Neutrophils arrive first, followed later by macrophages.

cards.front: How does inflammation produce fever?
cards.back: Interleukin-1 and interleukin-6 act through prostaglandin E2 to raise the hypothalamic temperature set point, so the body actively heats itself to the new target.

cards.front: Define shock in one sentence, and why is blood pressure a poor early marker?
cards.back: Shock is inadequate oxygen delivery to tissue for its needs. Sympathetic compensation holds blood pressure normal until roughly 30% of volume is lost, especially in young patients.

cards.front: What are the findings of compensated shock?
cards.back: Tachycardia, cool pale clammy skin, anxiety or restlessness, a narrowing pulse pressure, and delayed capillary refill, all with a near-normal systolic blood pressure.

cards.front: Why does lactate rise in shock, and what levels matter?
cards.back: Cells without oxygen burn glucose anaerobically and produce lactate. Over 2 mmol/L is abnormal, over 4 mmol/L is severe, and failure to clear it predicts death.

cards.front: Name the four families of shock and one cause of each.
cards.back: Hypovolemic (hemorrhage), cardiogenic (large myocardial infarction), obstructive (tension pneumothorax), distributive (sepsis, anaphylaxis, spinal cord injury).

cards.front: Why is a fluid bolus harmful in cardiogenic shock?
cards.back: The pump is already failing against high filling pressures that are backing up into the lungs. More preload worsens pulmonary edema without improving output.

cards.front: Name the three causes of obstructive shock and the fix for each.
cards.back: Cardiac tamponade (pericardiocentesis), tension pneumothorax (needle decompression), massive pulmonary embolism (thrombolysis or thrombectomy). Fluids and pressors only buy time.

cards.front: How does neurogenic shock differ from every other type?
cards.back: Loss of sympathetic outflow above roughly T6 causes hypotension with bradycardia and warm dry skin, instead of the tachycardia and cold clammy skin of other shock states.

cards.front: Why do the kidneys and gut fail first in prolonged shock?
cards.back: Compensation deliberately shunts blood away from kidney and splanchnic beds to protect brain and heart, so they are the first to be ischemic and the first to fail.

cards.front: What is the Sepsis-3 definition of sepsis?
cards.back: Suspected or documented infection plus organ dysfunction, quantified as an increase of 2 or more points in the SOFA score. The old SIRS criteria are a screen, not a definition.

cards.front: What defines septic shock, and what is its mortality?
cards.back: Sepsis requiring a vasopressor to keep mean arterial pressure at 65 mmHg or higher after adequate fluids, with a lactate above 2 mmol/L. Mortality is roughly 40%.

cards.front: How do cytokines cause hypotension in sepsis?
cards.back: They trigger massive nitric oxide production, which relaxes vascular smooth muscle everywhere, and they make capillaries leak plasma into the interstitium, so the container enlarges as the volume drains.

cards.front: Why are fluids given before vasopressors in septic shock?
cards.back: Sepsis causes real and relative hypovolemia, so squeezing an underfilled circulation raises the blood pressure number while reducing actual tissue flow. 30 mL/kg of crystalloid comes first.

cards.front: Why is a MAP of 65 mmHg the target in septic shock?
cards.back: Below roughly 65 mmHg the autoregulation that protects kidney and brain perfusion fails, so flow becomes directly dependent on pressure and organs begin to infarct.

cards.front: Why does lactate rise in sepsis even when perfusion looks adequate?
cards.back: Two reasons: tissue hypoperfusion drives anaerobic metabolism, and sepsis directly impairs mitochondrial use of oxygen, so cells make lactate despite delivered oxygen.

cards.front: What does the first-hour sepsis bundle contain?
cards.back: Lactate and blood cultures drawn, broad-spectrum antibiotics given, 30 mL/kg crystalloid for hypotension or lactate above 4, vasopressors for MAP under 65, and a repeat lactate.

cards.front: Why can a septic patient have warm, flushed skin and still be in shock?
cards.back: Early distributive shock has high cardiac output and dilated vessels, so skin is warm and pulses bound while tissue extraction fails. It turns cold and clamped late, once the heart is depressed.

cards.front: What makes a coronary plaque vulnerable to rupture?
cards.back: A thin fibrous cap over a large soft lipid core with active inflammation. Degree of narrowing matters less, which is why many infarcts come from 40-60% lesions.

cards.front: What happens in the seconds after a plaque cap tears?
cards.back: Blood contacts collagen and tissue factor, platelets adhere and activate and recruit more platelets, and the coagulation cascade lays fibrin over the plug, occluding the artery.

cards.front: Differentiate unstable angina, NSTEMI, and STEMI.
cards.back: Unstable angina: partial occlusion, ischemia without necrosis, troponin normal. NSTEMI: inner-layer necrosis, troponin elevated, no ST elevation. STEMI: persistent complete occlusion, full-thickness necrosis, ST elevation.

cards.front: Give troponin kinetics and explain why two values are drawn.
cards.back: Detectable in 1-4 hours, peaks at 12-24 hours, stays elevated 7-10 days. A rising or falling delta between samples means acute injury; a flat elevation usually means chronic disease.

cards.front: Name four mechanical complications of myocardial infarction and their timing.
cards.back: Ventricular fibrillation in the first hours, cardiogenic shock when over 40% of the left ventricle is lost, papillary muscle rupture at days 3-5, free wall rupture at days 3-7.

cards.front: How does an embolic stroke differ in onset from a thrombotic one?
cards.back: Embolic strokes, often from atrial fibrillation, are maximal at onset because the artery blocks instantly. Thrombotic strokes on local plaque tend to stutter or worsen over minutes to hours.

cards.front: What is the ischemic penumbra?
cards.back: Brain tissue around the dead core that is underperfused but still alive on collateral flow. It can recover if flow returns, and it is why roughly 1.9 million neurons are lost per untreated minute.

cards.front: Why is high blood pressure tolerated in acute ischemic stroke?
cards.back: Autoregulation is lost, so penumbral perfusion depends directly on systemic pressure. Thresholds are roughly 220/120, tightened to 185/110 if thrombolytics are given.

cards.front: Contrast HFrEF and HFpEF.
cards.back: HFrEF is a squeeze failure with a dilated weak ventricle ejecting under 40%. HFpEF is a filling failure with a thick stiff ventricle and a normal ejection fraction, typical of the older hypertensive patient.

cards.front: Which findings are left-sided heart failure and which are right-sided?
cards.back: Left backs up into lungs: breathlessness, orthopnea, waking gasping, crackles, pink frothy sputum. Right backs up into the body: distended neck veins, tender liver, ascites, leg edema.

cards.front: What is the most common cause of right-sided heart failure?
cards.back: Left-sided heart failure, because chronic pulmonary congestion raises the pressure the right ventricle must work against. Right failure from primary lung disease is called cor pulmonale.

cards.front: What does BNP measure and how is it interpreted?
cards.back: A hormone released by stretched ventricular muscle. Under 100 pg/mL argues against acute heart failure; above 400-500 supports it. Obesity falsely lowers it, kidney disease falsely raises it.

cards.front: Why do the body's compensations worsen heart failure?
cards.back: Sympathetic drive raises oxygen demand and shortens diastolic filling, while the RAAS retains salt and water and constricts vessels, increasing both preload and afterload on an already failing pump.

cards.front: Why do drugs that block compensation improve survival in heart failure?
cards.back: ACE inhibitors, ARBs, beta blockers, and aldosterone antagonists interrupt the loops that drive remodeling. Drugs that stimulate the heart relieve symptoms but shorten life.

cards.front: What is flash pulmonary edema and why is it treated differently?
cards.back: A sudden afterload spike stops a stiff ventricle ejecting, and pressure floods alveoli within minutes. The fluid is misplaced rather than excessive, so positive pressure ventilation and nitroglycerin come before diuresis.

cards.front: Distinguish type 1 and type 2 respiratory failure by numbers.
cards.back: Type 1 is hypoxemic: PaO2 below 60 mmHg, an oxygenation problem. Type 2 is hypercapnic: PaCO2 above 45 mmHg, a ventilation or pump problem.

cards.front: What is a shunt, and why does it not respond well to oxygen?
cards.back: Blood flows past alveoli that receive no ventilation at all, so it never contacts the supplemental oxygen and returns to the arterial side unchanged. Pneumonia, ARDS, and atelectasis cause it.

cards.front: Define ARDS and its ventilation strategy.
cards.back: Onset within a week of an insult, bilateral infiltrates not from heart failure, and a PaO2 to FiO2 ratio of 300 or less. Treat with low tidal volumes around 6 mL/kg predicted body weight.

cards.front: How does a large pulmonary embolism actually kill a patient?
cards.back: By obstructive shock, not hypoxemia alone. Blocked outflow raises right ventricular afterload, the thin right ventricle dilates and fails, the septum bows left, and the left ventricle cannot fill.

cards.front: What blood gas pattern is typical in pulmonary embolism?
